claim: Rising and more variable global temperatures pose a challenge for biodiversity.
source: Rising and more variable global temperatures pose a challenge for biodiversity, with reproduction and fertility being especially sensitive to heat.
evidence: This is a general statement about climate change impacts that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Reproduction and fertility are especially sensitive to heat.
source: Rising and more variable global temperatures pose a challenge for biodiversity, with reproduction and fertility being especially sensitive to heat.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about thermal sensitivity of reproductive processes.

claim: Following temperature increases through adult development, males produce shorter sperm.
source: Following temperature increases through adult development, we found opposing gamete responses, with males producing shorter sperm and females laying larger eggs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Following temperature increases through adult development, females lay larger eggs.
source: Following temperature increases through adult development, we found opposing gamete responses, with males producing shorter sperm and females laying larger eggs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gamete phenotypic plasticity in response to temperature is adaptive.
source: Importantly, this gamete phenotypic plasticity was adaptive: thermal translocation experiments showed that both sperm and eggs produced in warmer conditions had superior reproductive performance in warmer environments, and vice versa for cooler production conditions and reproductive environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from thermal translocation experiments.

claim: Sperm and eggs produced in warmer conditions have superior reproductive performance in warmer environments.
source: Importantly, this gamete phenotypic plasticity was adaptive: thermal translocation experiments showed that both sperm and eggs produced in warmer conditions had superior reproductive performance in warmer environments, and vice versa for cooler production conditions and reproductive environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from thermal translocation experiments.

claim: Sperm and eggs produced in cooler conditions have superior reproductive performance in cooler environments.
source: Importantly, this gamete phenotypic plasticity was adaptive: thermal translocation experiments showed that both sperm and eggs produced in warmer conditions had superior reproductive performance in warmer environments, and vice versa for cooler production conditions and reproductive environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from thermal translocation experiments.

claim: In warmer environments, gamete plasticity enables males to double their reproductive success.
source: In warmer environments, gamete plasticity enabled males to double their reproductive success, and females could increase offspring production by one-third.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data measuring reproductive output.

claim: In warmer environments, gamete plasticity enables females to increase offspring production by one-third.
source: In warmer environments, gamete plasticity enabled males to double their reproductive success, and females could increase offspring production by one-third.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data measuring offspring production.

claim: Adaptive phenotypic plasticity across a range of biological traits enables individuals to cope with fluctuating environments.
source: Adaptive phenotypic plasticity across a range of biological traits, from individual cell form and function to advanced learning, enables individuals to cope with fluctuating environments (Pigliucci, 2001; Miner et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Adaptive plasticity in behaviour, morphology and physiology is well-recognised in the diploid life stage.
source: This flexibility is well-recognised in the diploid life stage, where a complex multicellular organism can generate adaptive plasticity in behaviour, morphology and physiology.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about phenotypic plasticity.

claim: Far less is known about plastic adaptive responses at the gamete stage compared to the diploid stage.
source: However, far less is known about what plastic adaptive responses are possible at the seemingly simple unicellular gamete stage, when environmental variation can be profound.
evidence: This is an inference based on the state of the literature.

claim: Sperm almost always operate after ejaculation and release in a non-self and demanding environment.
source: Sperm almost always operate after ejaculation and release in a non-self and demanding environment, either within the female reproductive tract or through external fertilisation, and many factors that directly influence sperm function can vary profoundly across these environments (Pitnick et al., 2009; Reinhardt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and general biological knowledge.

claim: Many factors that directly influence sperm function can vary profoundly across reproductive environments.
source: Sperm almost always operate after ejaculation and release in a non-self and demanding environment, either within the female reproductive tract or through external fertilisation, and many factors that directly influence sperm function can vary profoundly across these environments (Pitnick et al., 2009; Reinhardt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ova face a challenging set of biotic and abiotic variables, especially in oviparous species.
source: Ova face a similarly challenging set of biotic and abiotic variables, especially in the many species that are oviparous where zygotes and embryos develop in eggs to hatch in the natural environment outside the mother (Hinton, 1981; Gilbert, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Temperature is one of the most important abiotic environmental variables.
source: One of the most important abiotic environmental variables is temperature (Cossins and Bowler, 1987; Angilletta Jr., 2009), especially in the context of climate change when thermal environments are expected to both warm and become much variable and extreme (Perkins et al., 2012; Raftery et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Thermal environments are expected to both warm and become much more variable and extreme under climate change.
source: One of the most important abiotic environmental variables is temperature (Cossins and Bowler, 1987; Angilletta Jr., 2009), especially in the context of climate change when thermal environments are expected to both warm and become much variable and extreme (Perkins et al., 2012; Raftery et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to climate change literature.

claim: Thermal variation has profound impacts on living systems.
source: Thermal variation has profound impacts on living systems, and numerous examples of adaptive plastic responses to temperature variability have been described, from acclimated mitochondrial function (Pichaud et al., 2010) and sex determination (Warner and Shine, 2008), up to complex shifts in behaviour (Pateman et al., 2012) and phenology (Walther et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Sperm production and function are especially sensitive to warming.
source: Temperature also influences gamete function across a number of levels, with sperm production and function being especially sensitive to warming (Setchell, 1998; Sales et al., 2018) and egg development being directly influenced by thermal regime (Gillooly et al., 2001; Gillooly et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Egg development is directly influenced by thermal regime.
source: Temperature also influences gamete function across a number of levels, with sperm production and function being especially sensitive to warming (Setchell, 1998; Sales et al., 2018) and egg development being directly influenced by thermal regime (Gillooly et al., 2001; Gillooly et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tribolium castaneum is ectothermic and oviparous like most sexually reproducing animals.
source: We test for this potential in the flour beetle Tribolium castaneum which, like most sexually reproducing animals, is both ectothermic and oviparous (Sokoloff, 1974), and in which spermatozoal sensitivity to temperature is known (Sales et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Spermatozoal sensitivity to temperature is known in Tribolium castaneum.
source: We test for this potential in the flour beetle Tribolium castaneum which, like most sexually reproducing animals, is both ectothermic and oviparous (Sokoloff, 1974), and in which spermatozoal sensitivity to temperature is known (Sales et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Thermal regime regulates gamete size development in the short-term.
source: We find that thermal regime regulates gamete size development: in the short-term, as the developmental environment warms, eggs get larger and sperm become smaller.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: As the developmental environment warms, eggs get larger.
source: We find that thermal regime regulates gamete size development: in the short-term, as the developmental environment warms, eggs get larger and sperm become smaller.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: As the developmental environment warms, sperm become smaller.
source: We find that thermal regime regulates gamete size development: in the short-term, as the developmental environment warms, eggs get larger and sperm become smaller.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Warmer reproductive environments present challenges for reproduction.
source: We find that warmer reproductive environments present challenges for reproduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced reproductive output at higher temperatures.

claim: Gamete plasticity enables significant improvements in reproductive performance.
source: However, gamete plasticity enabled significant improvements in reproductive performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from thermal translocation experiments.

claim: Adaptive thermal plasticity in gametes provides a route for ectothermic populations to buffer reproductive output against climate change.
source: Our findings reveal a potentially important route by which ectothermic populations can buffer their reproductive output against increasingly stressful and unpredictable temperature fluctuations under climate change.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Following 54 generations of experimental evolution at 38°C, males produce significantly longer sperm than males from lines evolved at 30°C.
source: Following 54 generations of experimental evolution under increased temperature, we found that at both development temperatures sperm length differed by an average of ~4% between long-term selection regimes, with males from lines evolved at 38°C producing significantly longer sperm than males from lines evolved at 30°C (effect size β = 3.4, t1,14 = 3.4, p=0.004; eight lines per regime, five males per line, and five sperm per male, Figure 2 and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Sperm length differs by an average of ~4% between long-term selection regimes at 30°C and 38°C.
source: Following 54 generations of experimental evolution under increased temperature, we found that at both development temperatures sperm length differed by an average of ~4% between long-term selection regimes, with males from lines evolved at 38°C producing significantly longer sperm than males from lines evolved at 30°C (effect size β = 3.4, t1,14 = 3.4, p=0.004; eight lines per regime, five males per line, and five sperm per male, Figure 2 and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: A within-generation increase in temperature during pupation and post-eclosion maturation reduces sperm length development irrespective of evolutionary background.
source: In contrast, a within-generation increase in temperature during pupation and post-eclosion maturation reduced sperm length development irrespective of evolutionary background, with sperm produced at 38°C being ~7% shorter, and indicating developmental plasticity in sperm size (β = −6.3, t1,24 = -11.2, p<0.001; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Sperm produced at 38°C are ~7% shorter than those produced at 30°C.
source: In contrast, a within-generation increase in temperature during pupation and post-eclosion maturation reduced sperm length development irrespective of evolutionary background, with sperm produced at 38°C being ~7% shorter, and indicating developmental plasticity in sperm size (β = −6.3, t1,24 = -11.2, p<0.001; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The interaction between selection regime and development environment on sperm length is not significant.
source: The interaction between selection regime and the development environment was not significant (β = 0.5, t1,24 = 0.4, p=0.672).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Male body sizes of 30°C and 38°C thermal selection lines do not differ.
source: Male body sizes of 30°C and 38°C thermal selection lines (TSLs) did not differ (F1,78 = 0.38, p=0.53), and similarly we found no evidence for body size divergence between 30°C or 38°C thermal environments from the pupal stage in the ancestral stock population (the Krakow Super Strain, KSS) (F1,46 = 0.90, p=0.35).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There is no evidence for body size divergence between 30°C or 38°C thermal environments from the pupal stage in the ancestral KSS population.
source: Male body sizes of 30°C and 38°C thermal selection lines (TSLs) did not differ (F1,78 = 0.38, p=0.53), and similarly we found no evidence for body size divergence between 30°C or 38°C thermal environments from the pupal stage in the ancestral stock population (the Krakow Super Strain, KSS) (F1,46 = 0.90, p=0.35).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Egg size shows an increase in response to a hotter proximate temperature.
source: Egg size also showed divergence and plasticity in relation to thermal regime. In contrast to sperm, egg size showed an increase in response to a hotter proximate temperature (β = 70.0, t1,14 = 13.9, p<0.001; Figure 3a and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a significant interaction between long-term selection regime and short-term temperature exposure on egg size.
source: However, there was a significant interaction between long-term selection regime and short-term temperature exposure (β = −25.7, t1,14 = -3.6, p=0.003; Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Following 58 generations of experimental evolution, eggs of females from TSLs evolved at 38°C are larger than those of 30°C TSL females when produced at 30°C.
source: Following 58 generations of experimental evolution (logistic contraints prevented simultaneous measurement at generation 54 when sperm lengths were assayed), eggs of females from TSLs evolved at 38°C were larger than those of 30°C TSL females when produced at 30°C (β = 23.0, t1,14 = 3.2, p=0.006), but were very similar in size when produced at 38°C (β = −2.8, t1,14 = -0.4, p=0.677).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Eggs from 38°C TSL females and 30°C TSL females are very similar in size when produced at 38°C.
source: Following 58 generations of experimental evolution (logistic contraints prevented simultaneous measurement at generation 54 when sperm lengths were assayed), eggs of females from TSLs evolved at 38°C were larger than those of 30°C TSL females when produced at 30°C (β = 23.0, t1,14 = 3.2, p=0.006), but were very similar in size when produced at 38°C (β = −2.8, t1,14 = -0.4, p=0.677).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Egg size is thermally plastic in standard ancestral stock KSS females.
source: Egg size was also thermally plastic in standard ancestral stock Krakow Super Strain (KSS) females, and showed significant divergence according to adult rearing and oviposition temperature when assessed in three experimental repeats.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: KSS females produce larger eggs when ovipositing at 38°C compared to 30°C.
source: KSS females produced larger eggs when ovipositing at 38°C compared to 30°C (β = 35.3, t1,356 = 8.2, p<0.001; 50 females per group and 60 eggs measured per group at either rearing temperature, Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Individual KSS females show egg size plasticity when ovipositing alone at either 30°C or 38°C.
source: In addition, this plasticity was shown by individual females ovipositing alone at either 30°C or 38°C (β = 81.5, t1,42 = 11.6, p<0.001; Figure 3c), and was reversible when females were alternated between 30°C and 38°C thermal environments (β = 58.9, t1,4 = 7.3, p=0.002; Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Egg size plasticity is reversible when females are alternated between 30°C and 38°C thermal environments.
source: In addition, this plasticity was shown by individual females ovipositing alone at either 30°C or 38°C (β = 81.5, t1,42 = 11.6, p<0.001; Figure 3c), and was reversible when females were alternated between 30°C and 38°C thermal environments (β = 58.9, t1,4 = 7.3, p=0.002; Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Egg width is not different between 30°C and 38°C oviposition temperatures.
source: Egg width was not different between the oviposition temperatures (F1,198 = 0.1, p=0.686, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2) and the interaction between oviposition temperature and egg length was not statistically significant (t = −0.77, p=0.44), demonstrating that oviposition temperature increased egg volumes (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for volume calculations).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Oviposition temperature increases egg volumes.
source: Egg width was not different between the oviposition temperatures (F1,198 = 0.1, p=0.686, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2) and the interaction between oviposition temperature and egg length was not statistically significant (t = −0.77, p=0.44), demonstrating that oviposition temperature increased egg volumes (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for volume calculations).
evidence: This is an inference based on the measurements of egg length and width.

claim: Sperm size is thermally plastic in ancestral stock KSS males.
source: As for the selection lines, sperm size was thermally plastic in ancestral stock KSS males, and showed significant divergence according to rearing temperatures (two experimental repeats), with KSS males producing significantly shorter sperm when reared at 38°C compared to 30°C (β = −5.1, t1,49 = -7.0, p<0.001; Figure 2b and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: KSS males produce significantly shorter sperm when reared at 38°C compared to 30°C.
source: As for the selection lines, sperm size was thermally plastic in ancestral stock KSS males, and showed significant divergence according to rearing temperatures (two experimental repeats), with KSS males producing significantly shorter sperm when reared at 38°C compared to 30°C (β = −5.1, t1,49 = -7.0, p<0.001; Figure 2b and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Reproduction is generally sensitive to the proximal thermal environment, with more offspring eclosing at 30°C than at 38°C.
source: Reproduction was generally sensitive to the proximal thermal environment, with on average 299 (± 20.8, mean ± s.e.m.) offspring eclosing at 30°C, compared with 135 (± 10.3, mean ± s.e.m.) at 38°C (β = −5.8, F1,104 = 69.8, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The thermal regime in which sperm production and insemination take place gives individual males a reproductive advantage when matched to the same thermal environment for fertilisation and offspring development.
source: Despite these overall differences, it was clear that the thermal regime in which sperm production and insemination took place also gave individual males a reproductive advantage when matched to the same thermal environment for fertilisation and offspring development (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The interaction between spermatogenesis temperature and offspring production temperature is highly significant.
source: Indeed, the interaction between spermatogenesis temperature (sperm production) and offspring production temperature was highly significant (β = 7.5, F1,104 = 29.6, p<0.001), while the main effect of male treatment was not significant (β = 0.7, F1,104 = 1.1, p=0.290).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Sperm from males exposed to 30°C achieve greater reproductive success in the 30°C reproductive environment than sperm from males that completed development at 38°C.
source: Sperm from males exposed as pupae and maturing adults to 30°C achieved greater reproductive success in the 30°C reproductive environment than sperm from males that completed development at 38°C.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In the 38°C reproductive environment, sperm produced by males in the 38°C treatment achieve double the reproductive success compared with sperm from males developed through the 30°C treatment.
source: By contrast, in the 38°C reproductive environment sperm produced by males in the 38°C treatment achieved double the reproductive success compared with sperm from males developed through the 30°C treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Across 100 days of oviposition in the 30°C reproductive environment, males reared at 30°C sired an average of 349 offspring while males reared at 38°C sired 249 offspring.
source: Across 100 days of oviposition in the 30°C reproductive environment, males reared at 30°C sired an average of 349 (± 29.1, mean ± s.e.m.) offspring, while males reared at 38°C sired 249 (± 27.1, mean ± s.e.m.) offspring.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In the 38°C reproductive environment, males reared at 38°C sired 180 offspring while males reared at 30°C sired only 91 offspring.
source: Using the same protocols in the 38°C reproductive environment, males reared at 38°C sired 180 (± 12, mean ± s.e.m. offspring), while males reared at 30°C sired only 91 (± 12, mean ± s.e.m.) offspring (Figure 4a and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Sperm matched to the fertilisation and development temperature consistently outperform sperm that are thermally mismatched.
source: Exploration of the temporal patterns of these effects showed a clear decline in reproduction across consecutive 10-day blocks, and that sperm matched to the fertilisation and development temperature consistently outperformed sperm that were thermally mismatched (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4b and c.

claim: There is a significant interaction between oviposition thermal regime and environmental temperature treatments on egg-to-adult offspring viability.
source: There was a significant interaction between oviposition thermal regime and the environmental temperature treatments at which the eggs were incubated, and offspring hatched and developed (z = −4.1, p<0.001; Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: At 30°C, eggs oviposited at 30°C achieve significantly greater egg-to-adult offspring viability rates than eggs oviposited at 38°C.
source: Post hoc testing showed that at 30°C eggs oviposited at 30°C achieved significantly greater egg-to-adult offspring viability rates than eggs oviposited at 38°C (z = 4.6, p<0.0001), whereas the opposite was true at 40°C (z = 3.01, p=0.01) where 30°C-oviposited eggs resulted in 25% fewer offspring than 38°C-oviposited eggs.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: At 40°C, 30°C-oviposited eggs result in 25% fewer offspring than 38°C-oviposited eggs.
source: Post hoc testing showed that at 30°C eggs oviposited at 30°C achieved significantly greater egg-to-adult offspring viability rates than eggs oviposited at 38°C (z = 4.6, p<0.0001), whereas the opposite was true at 40°C (z = 3.01, p=0.01) where 30°C-oviposited eggs resulted in 25% fewer offspring than 38°C-oviposited eggs.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the 38°C environment, there is no evidence for adaptive plasticity in egg biology.
source: In the 38°C environment, there was no evidence for any adaptive plasticity in egg biology, with the same relative number of eggs from the 30°C and 38°C regime females hatching and producing adult offspring (Figure 5 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Gamete function and reproduction is highly sensitive to the local thermal environment.
source: Our experiments revealed that: (1) gamete function and reproduction is highly sensitive to the local thermal environment; (2) developmental plasticity exists within sperm and eggs in response to temperature; (3) plastic responses in gamete size proceed in different directions in either sex; and (4) gamete plasticity is adaptive, enabling males and females to significantly improve their reproductive success via mechanisms that match sperm and egg development to the imminent thermal environment in which they must function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Developmental plasticity exists within sperm and eggs in response to temperature.
source: Our experiments revealed that: (1) gamete function and reproduction is highly sensitive to the local thermal environment; (2) developmental plasticity exists within sperm and eggs in response to temperature; (3) plastic responses in gamete size proceed in different directions in either sex; and (4) gamete plasticity is adaptive, enabling males and females to significantly improve their reproductive success via mechanisms that match sperm and egg development to the imminent thermal environment in which they must function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Plastic responses in gamete size proceed in different directions in either sex.
source: Our experiments revealed that: (1) gamete function and reproduction is highly sensitive to the local thermal environment; (2) developmental plasticity exists within sperm and eggs in response to temperature; (3) plastic responses in gamete size proceed in different directions in either sex; and (4) gamete plasticity is adaptive, enabling males and females to significantly improve their reproductive success via mechanisms that match sperm and egg development to the imminent thermal environment in which they must function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing opposing size changes in sperm and eggs.

claim: Gamete plasticity enables males and females to significantly improve their reproductive success via mechanisms that match sperm and egg development to the imminent thermal environment.
source: Our experiments revealed that: (1) gamete function and reproduction is highly sensitive to the local thermal environment; (2) developmental plasticity exists within sperm and eggs in response to temperature; (3) plastic responses in gamete size proceed in different directions in either sex; and (4) gamete plasticity is adaptive, enabling males and females to significantly improve their reproductive success via mechanisms that match sperm and egg development to the imminent thermal environment in which they must function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from thermal translocation experiments.

claim: Sperm production and function is affected by many environmental variables.
source: Sperm production and function is known to be affected by many environmental variables (Pitnick et al., 2009; Reinhardt et al., 2015), with particular sensitivities to temperature (Setchell, 1998; David et al., 2005), which may be especially important in ectotherms where environmental temperature varies through the reproductive window (Reinhardt et al., 2015; Walsh et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Environmental temperature variation is especially important in ectotherms where temperature varies through the reproductive window.
source: Sperm production and function is known to be affected by many environmental variables (Pitnick et al., 2009; Reinhardt et al., 2015), with particular sensitivities to temperature (Setchell, 1998; David et al., 2005), which may be especially important in ectotherms where environmental temperature varies through the reproductive window (Reinhardt et al., 2015; Walsh et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Temperature variation directly influences important elements within the sperm storage and fertilisation environment.
source: Such variation will directly influence important elements within the sperm storage and fertilisation environment (Pitnick et al., 2009; Reinhardt et al., 2015), including biophysical properties of fluids and membranes (Kupriyanova and Havenhand, 2005), mitochondrial metabolic sensitivity (Sokolova, 2018), flagellar function (Humphries, 2013) and haplotype integrity (Paul et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transplant experiments reveal obvious challenges for gamete performance in warmer environments, with an overall halving of reproductive output when sperm and eggs function at 38°C versus 30°C.
source: Our transplant experiments reveal obvious challenges for gamete performance in warmer environments, with an overall halving of reproductive output when sperm and eggs are challenged to function at 38°C versus 30°C (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Between-line variance in sperm length increases when males are forced to develop sperm at 38°C.
source: Interestingly, between-line variance in sperm length also increased when males were forced to develop sperm at 38°C (Figure 2a and b), possibly indicating a response to thermal stress at the higher temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2, with speculation about the cause.

claim: Increased metabolic and developmental rates in the 38°C regime may have elevated mating activity and promoted selection for increased sperm length.
source: Recent work examining sperm length evolution in T. castaneum revealed that a history of heightened sexual selection led to the evolution of longer sperm (Godwin et al., 2017), so one possibility is that increased metabolic and developmental rates in the 38°C regime had elevated mating activity, and therefore promoted male-male competition and selection for increased sperm length.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern, citing previous work.

claim: A history of heightened sexual selection leads to the evolution of longer sperm in T. castaneum.
source: Recent work examining sperm length evolution in T. castaneum revealed that a history of heightened sexual selection led to the evolution of longer sperm (Godwin et al., 2017), so one possibility is that increased metabolic and developmental rates in the 38°C regime had elevated mating activity, and therefore promoted male-male competition and selection for increased sperm length.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Warmer conditions generally reduce male reproductive fitness.
source: However, our current results (Figure 4) and past findings (Sales et al., 2018) indicate that warmer conditions generally reduce male reproductive fitness, and we find no evidence that operational sex ratios have deviated between our 30°C or 38°C selection line regimes, with both showing an average adult sex ratio of 50% (54 adults randomly sampled from six lines per regime: 30°C regime male ratios = 0.52, 0.46, 0.50, 0.52, 0.48, 0.52; 38°C regime male ratios = 0.50, 0.59, 0.48, 0.48, 0.52, 0.43); offspring sex ratios are also not changed following male exposure to 42°C heatwaves (Sales, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by current experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: Operational sex ratios have not deviated between 30°C or 38°C selection line regimes, with both showing an average adult sex ratio of 50%.
source: However, our current results (Figure 4) and past findings (Sales et al., 2018) indicate that warmer conditions generally reduce male reproductive fitness, and we find no evidence that operational sex ratios have deviated between our 30°C or 38°C selection line regimes, with both showing an average adult sex ratio of 50% (54 adults randomly sampled from six lines per regime: 30°C regime male ratios = 0.52, 0.46, 0.50, 0.52, 0.48, 0.52; 38°C regime male ratios = 0.50, 0.59, 0.48, 0.48, 0.52, 0.43); offspring sex ratios are also not changed following male exposure to 42°C heatwaves (Sales, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Offspring sex ratios are not changed following male exposure to 42°C heatwaves.
source: However, our current results (Figure 4) and past findings (Sales et al., 2018) indicate that warmer conditions generally reduce male reproductive fitness, and we find no evidence that operational sex ratios have deviated between our 30°C or 38°C selection line regimes, with both showing an average adult sex ratio of 50% (54 adults randomly sampled from six lines per regime: 30°C regime male ratios = 0.52, 0.46, 0.50, 0.52, 0.48, 0.52; 38°C regime male ratios = 0.50, 0.59, 0.48, 0.48, 0.52, 0.43); offspring sex ratios are also not changed following male exposure to 42°C heatwaves (Sales, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: T. castaneum is a relatively long-lived insect, with adult males showing no change in fertility even after one year of lifespan.
source: However, T. castaneum is a relatively long-lived insect, with adult males showing no change in fertility even after one year of lifespan (Godwin, 2016), so reproductive ageing differences over the few days of the sperm length assays conducted here are unlikely to explain the overall sperm length increases in the thermal selection lines at 38°C.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Temperature variation during gametogenesis affects sperm size in ectotherms.
source: Temperature variation during gametogenesis is known to affect sperm size in ectotherms (Blanckenhorn and Hellriegel, 2002; Rohmer et al., 2004), and cool and warm thermal extremes can reduce fertile function in tandem with reduced sperm length development (Vasudeva et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cool and warm thermal extremes can reduce fertile function in tandem with reduced sperm length development.
source: Temperature variation during gametogenesis is known to affect sperm size in ectotherms (Blanckenhorn and Hellriegel, 2002; Rohmer et al., 2004), and cool and warm thermal extremes can reduce fertile function in tandem with reduced sperm length development (Vasudeva et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Adaptive plasticity in the production of sperm numbers is known in relation to environmental risks of male-male competition.
source: Adaptive plasticity in the production of sperm numbers is known in relation to environmental risks of male-male competition (Wedell et al., 2002), with the capability for spermatogenesis to increase in response to elevated risks of sperm competition (Ramm and Stockley, 2009; Giannakara et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Spermatogenesis can increase in response to elevated risks of sperm competition.
source: Adaptive plasticity in the production of sperm numbers is known in relation to environmental risks of male-male competition (Wedell et al., 2002), with the capability for spermatogenesis to increase in response to elevated risks of sperm competition (Ramm and Stockley, 2009; Giannakara et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Domestic cockerels rapidly change their sperm mobility in relation to their own competitive status.
source: This male plasticity can also change individual sperm cell form and function: domestic cockerels (Gallus gallus domesticus) rapidly changed their sperm mobility in relation to their own competitive status (Pizzari et al., 2007), and male Gouldian finches (Erythrura gouldiae) adjusted sperm morphometry in relation to social factors (Immler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Male Gouldian finches adjust sperm morphometry in relation to social factors.
source: This male plasticity can also change individual sperm cell form and function: domestic cockerels (Gallus gallus domesticus) rapidly changed their sperm mobility in relation to their own competitive status (Pizzari et al., 2007), and male Gouldian finches (Erythrura gouldiae) adjusted sperm morphometry in relation to social factors (Immler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sperm velocity and density change in Arctic charr when dominance switches.
source: Similar changes occured in sperm velocity and density in Arctic charr (Salvelinus alpinus) when dominance switched (Rudolfsen et al., 2006), and broadcast-spawning ascidians (Styela plicata) produced larger, more motile sperm when adults were kept at densities with greater risks of sperm competition (Crean and Marshall, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Broadcast-spawning ascidians produce larger, more motile sperm when adults are kept at densities with greater risks of sperm competition.
source: Similar changes occured in sperm velocity and density in Arctic charr (Salvelinus alpinus) when dominance switched (Rudolfsen et al., 2006), and broadcast-spawning ascidians (Styela plicata) produced larger, more motile sperm when adults were kept at densities with greater risks of sperm competition (Crean and Marshall, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Acclimation experiments with the tubeworm Hydroides diramphus revealed adaptive plasticity in sperm and egg function in relation to salinity.
source: Acclimation and in vitro fertilisation experiments with the broadcast spawning tubeworm Hydroides diramphus revealed adaptive plasticity in sperm and egg function in relation to salinity, with gametes performing best at salinities experienced by their parents prior to spawning (Jensen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sticklebacks show adaptive plasticity in spermatozoal sensitivity to the salinity and osmolarity signal for initiating flagellar motility.
source: Likewise, sticklebacks (Gasterosteus aculeatus) showed adaptive plasticity in spermatozoal sensitivity to the salinity and osmolarity signal for initiating flagellar motility (Taugbøl et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Male mosquitofish acclimated to cool and warm regimes showed no signs of spermatozoal acclimation or change in thermal limits.
source: To our knowledge, only two studies have investigated sperm plasticity in relation to temperature: male mosquitofish (Gambusia holbrooki) acclimated to cool (18°C) and warm (30°C) regimes for five weeks showed no signs of spermatozoal acclimation or change in thermal limits (Adriaenssens et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Warm conditions reduce sperm motility in brown trout, but warm-acclimated males do not produce sperm with improved relative motility.
source: Likewise, although warm conditions reduced sperm motility in brown trout (Salmo trutta), warm-acclimated males did not produce sperm with improved relative motility (Fenkes et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Males exposed to warmer 38°C temperatures produce sperm that enable a doubling of reproductive success in warmer 38°C fertilisation and reproductive environments compared with sperm produced at 30°C.
source: Our transplant experiments revealed clear evidence for adaptive developmental plasticity in sperm function according to thermal regime, with males exposed to warmer 38°C temperatures producing sperm that enabled a doubling of reproductive success in warmer 38°C fertilisation and reproductive environments compared with sperm produced at 30°C (Figure 4a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and c.

claim: Sperm produced in cooler 30°C regimes gain ~40% greater reproductive success at 30°C compared with sperm produced at 38°C.
source: The opposite also applied, with sperm produced in cooler 30°C regimes gaining ~40% greater reproductive success at 30°C compared with sperm produced at 38°C (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: Sperm production takes around four days at 30°C in T. castaneum.
source: Sperm manufacture proceeds rapidly in T. castaneum, with production of mature, functional gametes taking around four days at 30°C (Fishman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Fertilisation and oviposition proceed within hours of mating in T. castaneum.
source: As in many insects, fertilisation and oviposition proceeds within hours of mating in T. castaneum (Fedina and Lewis, 2008), so sperm production temperature will usually predict insemination, storage and fertilisation temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sperm production temperature usually predicts insemination, storage and fertilisation temperature in T. castaneum.
source: As in many insects, fertilisation and oviposition proceeds within hours of mating in T. castaneum (Fedina and Lewis, 2008), so sperm production temperature will usually predict insemination, storage and fertilisation temperature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid timing of fertilisation after mating.

claim: Female T. castaneum produce larger gametes in the warmer environment, which is unusual for arthropods.
source: In contrast to males, female T. castaneum produced larger gametes in the warmer environment (Figure 3), which is unusual for arthropods where smaller eggs are usually produced as temperatures increase (Fox and Czesak, 2000); but see Seko and Nakasuji (2006) and Stillwell and Fox (2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: Smaller eggs are usually produced as temperatures increase in arthropods.
source: In contrast to males, female T. castaneum produced larger gametes in the warmer environment (Figure 3), which is unusual for arthropods where smaller eggs are usually produced as temperatures increase (Fox and Czesak, 2000); but see Seko and Nakasuji (2006) and Stillwell and Fox (2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Egg size plasticity occurs within two days of exposure to a novel thermal regime.
source: This egg size plasticity occurred within two days of exposure to the novel thermal regime, and was reversible (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: 36% of eggs produced at 38°C generate viable offspring following development at 40°C compared with only 27% of eggs produced at 30°C.
source: Egg plasticity was also adaptive when comparing performance between the more extreme 30°C versus 40°C environments (Figure 5): 36% of eggs produced at 38°C generated viable offspring following development at 40°C compared with only 27% of eggs produced at 30°C.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: 90% of eggs produced at 30°C generate offspring when developed at 30°C, versus 80% of eggs developed at 38°C.
source: Conversely, 90% of eggs produced at 30°C generated offspring when developed at 30°C, versus 80% of eggs developed at 38°C (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Adaptive plasticity in egg biology in relation to biotic variation is shown by seed beetles, where females vary egg size in relation to anticipated host plant quality.
source: Adaptive egg plasticity in relation to biotic variation is shown by seed beetles (Stator limbatus), where females vary egg size in relation to anticipated host plant quality (Fox et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Female cowpea weevils lay larger eggs to improve larval fitness in response to predicted levels of larval competition.
source: Likewise, female cowpea weevils (Callosobruchus maculatus) are sensitive to levels of larval competition predicted by increased adult density, laying larger eggs to improve larval fitness (Kawecki, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Broadcast-spawning ascidians produce smaller eggs in high density populations, but their embryo-yielding ovicells are larger than eggs from low-density adults.
source: Broadcast-spawning ascidians (S. plicata) produce smaller eggs in high density populations, but their embryo-yielding ovicells are larger than eggs from low-density adults (Crean and Marshall, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Female Nasonia vitripennis wasps adjust the sex ratio of their broods depending on whether they are first or second to parasitise a host.
source: Similarly, female Nasonia vitripennis wasps adjust the sex ratio of their broods depending on whether they are first or second to parasitise a host, improving offspring fitness according to anticipated variation in local mate competition (Werren, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Female stink bugs detect reflectance at the site where they oviposit and invest more protective pigment into eggs that will be exposed to stronger ultraviolet solar radiation.
source: Female stink bugs (Podisus maculiventris) detect reflectance at the site where they oviposit, and invest more protective pigment into eggs that will be exposed to stronger ultraviolet solar radiation (Abram et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Bicyclus anynana butterfly females lay larger (and fewer) eggs when exposed to lower temperatures during oviposition.
source: A notable exception is in Bicyclus anynana butterflies, where females lay larger (and fewer) eggs when they are exposed to lower temperatures during oviposition (Fischer et al., 2003a); reciprocal transfer experiments, as we employ here, show that this behaviour is adaptive (Fischer et al., 2003b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Adaptive matching through warmer egg development temperatures enables a 33% improvement in offspring production in the hottest reproductive environment.
source: We identify adaptive plasticity in response to the upper ranges of reproductive tolerance by T. castaneum females, with adaptive matching through warmer egg development temperatures enabling a 33% improvement in offspring production in the hottest reproductive environment (Table 2, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2 and Figure 5.

claim: Changes in sperm physiology, rather than morphometry, likely allow plasticity in sperm function to match thermal reproductive environments.
source: It therefore seems more likely that changes in sperm physiology, rather than morphometry, allow plasticity in sperm function to match thermal reproductive environments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that sperm size changes do not correlate with improved performance.

claim: Thermal adaptations influencing cell physiology and biochemistry exist within mitochondrial metabolism.
source: Thermal adaptations influencing cell physiology and biochemistry are known to exist within mitochondrial metabolism (Egginton and Sidell, 1989; Guderley and St-Pierre, 2002), essential for sperm function (Ramalho-Santos et al., 2009), and membrane properties influencing cell structure and physiology (Cossins and Prosser, 1978) for sperm and flagellum function (Cardullo and Wolf, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mitochondrial metabolism is essential for sperm function.
source: Thermal adaptations influencing cell physiology and biochemistry are known to exist within mitochondrial metabolism (Egginton and Sidell, 1989; Guderley and St-Pierre, 2002), essential for sperm function (Ramalho-Santos et al., 2009), and membrane properties influencing cell structure and physiology (Cossins and Prosser, 1978) for sperm and flagellum function (Cardullo and Wolf, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Heat Shock Proteins are expressed throughout spermatogenesis in the testis and play key roles in sperm development.
source: In addition, Heat Shock Proteins, expressed throughout spermatogenesis in the testis, play key roles in sperm development (Dun et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Within-ejaculate haplotype selection provides a mechanism for improving offspring performance.
source: Within-ejaculate haplotype selection provides another mechanism for improving offspring performance (Alavioon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Larger-volume eggs produced at higher temperatures contain more fluids and possibly a greater nutrient load, which could improve offspring viability under heat stress and desiccation.
source: Adaptive thermal plasticity may be possible via changes in egg size, because larger-volume eggs produced at higher temperatures will contain more fluids, and possibly a greater nutrient load, both of which could improve offspring viability under heat stress and desiccation (Fischer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Increased loading of HSP23 into D. melanogaster eggs improves embryo thermal tolerance.
source: Heat Shock Proteins could also play vital roles in protecting egg development from thermal stress; recent work demonstrates that increased loading of HSP23 into D. melanogaster eggs improves embryo thermal tolerance (Lockwood et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The potential for adaptive transgenerational plasticity via the matriline and through transcription factors within eggs is increasingly recognised.
source: The potential for adaptive transgenerational plasticity via the matriline and through transcription factors within eggs is increasingly recognised (Ho and Burggren, 2010), potentially enabling rapid responses to climate change via adaptive plasticity (Diamond, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is growing evidence that sperm have the potential to be transcriptionally labile.
source: There is growing evidence that sperm also have the potential to be transcriptionally labile (Immler, 2018), passing environmentally-driven epigenetic information to offspring through histone or protamine modifications, haplotype DNA methylation remodelling, and/or small RNAs (Donkin and Barrès, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sperm carry complex payloads of coding and non-coding small RNAs which can be transcribed into the oocyte and embryo.
source: Sperm carry complex payloads of coding and non-coding small RNAs which can be transcribed into the oocyte and embryo (Dadoune, 2009; Hosken and Hodgson, 2014) with conserved functions across mammalian and insect models (Fischer et al., 2012); the potential importance of these RNA transcripts remains largely unexplored (Carrell, 2008; Carone et al., 2010; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The potential importance of sperm RNA transcripts remains largely unexplored.
source: Sperm carry complex payloads of coding and non-coding small RNAs which can be transcribed into the oocyte and embryo (Dadoune, 2009; Hosken and Hodgson, 2014) with conserved functions across mammalian and insect models (Fischer et al., 2012); the potential importance of these RNA transcripts remains largely unexplored (Carrell, 2008; Carone et al., 2010; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transgenerational information transmission via sperm or egg epigenomes in response to environmental variation during gametogenesis is a possible mechanism to enable adaptive thermal plasticity under climate change.
source: However, the possibility for transgenerational information transmission via sperm or egg epigenomes in response to environmental variation during gametogenesis is an obvious mechanism to enable adaptive thermal plasticity for populations facing the challenge of reproducing under climate change where increases in both thermal averages, maxima and variation are expected (Perkins et al., 2012; Raftery et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms, supported by citations about climate change.

claim: The optimum laboratory temperature for population productivity in T. castaneum is 35°C.
source: 30°C is our standard rearing temperature, and the optimum laboratory temperature for population productivity in T. castaneum is 35°C (Sokoloff, 1974; Sales, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 38°C approaches the upper thermal limit across more sensitive juvenile stages in T. castaneum.
source: 38°C approaches the upper thermal limit across more sensitive juvenile stages (Dickinson, 2018; Sales, 2019), and this temperature has been recorded in 150 countries (Mherrera, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 38°C has been recorded in 150 countries.
source: 38°C approaches the upper thermal limit across more sensitive juvenile stages (Dickinson, 2018; Sales, 2019), and this temperature has been recorded in 150 countries (Mherrera, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Heatwaves are predicted to increase in frequency, severity and duration under climate change.
source: Our experimental exposure to this thermal regime will have relevance to more extreme thermal conditions and heatwaves, predicted to increase in frequency, severity and duration under climate change (e.g. Perkins et al., 2012), and which we know specifically constrain reproduction and sperm function in this system (Sales et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Heatwaves specifically constrain reproduction and sperm function in T. castaneum.
source: Our experimental exposure to this thermal regime will have relevance to more extreme thermal conditions and heatwaves, predicted to increase in frequency, severity and duration under climate change (e.g. Perkins et al., 2012), and which we know specifically constrain reproduction and sperm function in this system (Sales et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Following a single mating period, female T. castaneum typically use up all viable sperm within 100 days.
source: To test for the adaptive value of any functional plasticity, the performance of sperm from males of the same ancestral KSS population reared from pupation at either 30°C or 38°C was tracked by comparing the total number of offspring sired across 100 days of oviposition by KSS females at either 30°C or 38°C (Figure 4a and Table 2), by which time all females in the experiment had exhausted their viable sperm stores (Michalczyk et al., 2010) and ceased to produce offspring (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.
